You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

What is the difference between a method and a function?

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

name: read
content:
1	Strings Are Immutable
     2	To wrap this section up, let’s discuss an important property of string
     3	objects. Strings are immutable, which means that you can’t change
     4	them once you’ve created them. For instance, see what happens when
     5	you try to assign a new letter to one particular character of a string:
     6	>>> word = "goal"
     7	>>> word[0] = "f"
     8	Traceback (most recent call last):
     9	File "<pyshell#16>", line 1, in <module>
    10	word[0] = "f"
    11	TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
    12	Python throws a TypeError and tells you that str objects don’t support
    13	item assignment.
    14	If you want to alter a string, then you must create an entirely new
    15	string. To change the string "goal" to the string "foal", you can use a
    16	string slice to concatenate the letter "f" with everything but the first
    17	letter of the word "goal":
    18	>>> word = "goal"
    19	>>> word = "f" + word[1:]
    20	>>> word
    21	'foal'
    22	First, you assign the string "goal" to the variable word. Then you concatenate the slice word[1:],
    23	which is the string "oal", with the letter "f"
    24	to get the string "foal". If you’re getting a different result here, then
    25	make sure you’re including the colon character (:) as part of the string
    26	slice.
    27	
    28	4.3 Manipulate Strings With Methods
    29	Strings come bundled with special functions called string methods
    30	that you can use to work with and manipulate strings. There are numerous string methods available,
    31	but we’ll focus on some of the most
    32	commonly used ones.
    33	In this section, you’ll learn how to:
    34	• Convert a string to uppercase or lowercase
    35	• Remove whitespace from a string
    36	• Determine if a string begins or ends with certain characters
    37	Let’s go!
    38	Converting String Case
    39	To convert a string to all lowercase letters, you use the string’s .lower()
    40	method. This is done by tacking .lower() onto the end of the string
    41	itself:
    42	>>> "Jean-Luc Picard".lower()
    43	'jean-luc picard'
    44	The dot (.) tells Python that what follows is the name of a method—
    45	the lower() method in this case.
    46	Note
    47	We’ll refer to string methods with a dot (.) at the beginning of
    48	their names. For example, .lower() is written with a leading dot
    49	instead of as lower().
    50	This makes it easier to differentiate functions that are string
    51	methods from built-in functions like print() and type().
    52	String methods don’t just work on string literals. You can also use
    53	.lower() on a string assigned to a variable:
    54	>>> name = "Jean-Luc Picard"
    55	>>> name.lower()
    56	'jean-luc picard'
    57	The opposite of .lower() is .upper(), which converts every character in
    58	a string to uppercase:
    59	>>> name.upper()
    60	'JEAN-LUC PICARD'
    61	Compare the .upper() and .lower() string methods to the len() function you saw in the last section.
    62	Aside from the different results of
    63	these functions, the important distinction here is how they’re used.
    64	len() is a stand-alone function. If you want to determine the length of
    65	the name string, then you call the len() function directly:
    66	>>> len(name)
    67	15
    68	On the other hand, .upper() and .lower() must be used in conjunction
    69	with a string. They do not exist independently.
    70	
    71	String Methods and Immutability
    72	Recall from the previous section that strings are immutable—they
    73	can’t be changed once they’ve been created. Most string methods
    74	that alter a string, like .upper() and .lower(), actually return copies of
    75	the original string with the appropriate modifications.
    76	If you aren’t careful, this can introduce subtle bugs into your program.
    77	Try this out in IDLE’s interactive window:
    78	>>> name = "Picard"
    79	>>> name.upper()
    80	'PICARD'
    81	>>> name
    82	'Picard'
    83	When you call name.upper(), nothing about name actually changes. If
    84	you need to keep the result, then you need to assign it to a variable:
    85	>>> name = "Picard"
    86	>>> name = name.upper()
    87	>>> name
    88	'PICARD'
    89	name.upper() returns a new string "PICARD", which is reassigned to the
    90	name variable. This overrides the original string "Picard" that you first
    91	assigned to name.

According to `doc.txt`, the difference is that methods are special functions that come bundled with strings and must be used in conjunction with a string, whereas functions like `len()` are stand-alone and called directly.

Specifically, the document says:

- "Strings come bundled with special functions called string methods that you can use to work with and manipulate strings." (doc.txt)
- "The dot (.) tells Python that what follows is the name of a method—the lower() method in this case." (doc.txt)
- "We’ll refer to string methods with a dot (.) at the beginning of their names. For example, .lower() is written with a leading dot instead of as lower(). This makes it easier to differentiate functions that are string methods from built-in functions like print() and type()." (doc.txt)
- "len() is a stand-alone function. If you want to determine the length of the name string, then you call the len() function directly." (doc.txt)
- "On the other hand, .upper() and .lower() must be used in conjunction with a string. They do not exist independently." (doc.txt)

So, in the document's terms: a method is a string-bundled function written with a leading dot that does not exist independently, while a function such as `len()` is stand-alone and called directly.
